extracted.intended_audience: translators, critics, and literary readers (especially of satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for translating and prefacing a satirical work (Rabelais) focusing on tone, fidelity, audience-management, and rhetorical strategy. Advises what pleases readers, how to render idiom and wit, and how a translator should comport themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of preface method (bully vs. wheedle)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two sorts of taking prefaces: (1) bully/railing at the audience to frighten them into complaisance, or (2) wheedling/flattery to win them over. Mr. Bays observed that if thunder and lightning could not frighten an audience, the sight of the poet with a rope might work them into pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bullying (railing) seldom works in the present age; wheedling is safer but must be particular rather than general. Choose method with awareness of its effects on readers and their sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of huffing and cringing (mixed preface tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: If neither bullying nor wheedling alone will work, blend the two into one: 'from this marriage of huffing and cringing, there will result a new kind of careless medley' which may please both sorts of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed tone can leverage novelty to win over both readers who like to be hectored and those who respond to flattery; use the mixture deliberately rather than clumsily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities that recommend a work
rubrics_metrics.description: If uncommon worth, lively wit, and deep learning, wove into wholesome satire, a bold, good, and vast design admirably pursued, truth set out in its true light, and a method how to arrive to its oracle, can recommend a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to combine substantive merit (worth, learning) with vivacity (wit), clear satirical purpose, ambitious design, and a demonstrable relation to truth; these are the chief recommenders to a reasonable reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's duty: give author's sense and copy style
rubrics_metrics.description: The translator has no share in the invention or disposition of the author's work; his proper praise is 'giving his author's sense in its full extent, and copying his style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize fidelity to the author's meaning and style rather than seeking personal credit or invention; translation is primarily representation, not authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render common talk naturally in the target language
rubrics_metrics.description: What seems most common talk in one language is often the most difficult to make so in another; it is hard to give the 'free easy air of an original.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to make colloquial passages read as if native in the target language: smooth obsolete turns, find idiomatic equivalents, and avoid literalism that betrays foreignness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of a foreigner's language-graces
rubrics_metrics.description: Every language has peculiar graces seldom or never to be acquired by a foreigner; the translator cannot hope to give all of the author's original linguistic graces in every place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be candid about inevitable losses; aim for naturalness and sense rather than futile attempts to replicate every local turn of phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive apology or self-importance in the preface
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers care no more for this or that apology of the translator if the version does not please them; the translator has no share in the invention, and should not pretend to much praise beyond faithful rendering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep preface concise and relevant; do not over-explain or over-praise your own labors—let the translation speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure targets of satire when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais studied to be dark and bedaub his book with loose expressions so he might not be thought to have any other design than to droll; this shields the author from enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satire risks retaliation, consider deliberate ambiguity or masking of targets; craft obscurity so the work can satirize safely while still entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and write for audience types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are readers to be hectored and readers to be creeped to; some will love 'witty mirth and a chirping bottle,' others (solid sots) will not be pleased. Critics vary: some rail in hope of fame, others flatter for favor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the likely audience (witty readers, critics, sober moralists) and modulate tone and content accordingly; accept that universal approval is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of such writings: diversion and comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Many languishing, sick, and disconsolate persons, perusing such fables, have deceived their grief, passed their time merrily, and been inspired with new joy and comfort; the author aimed to give little help by his pen to those in affliction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember the remedial/social purpose of comic and satirical works — to divert, comfort, and restore cheer — and let this aim inform translation and prefatory remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle coarse or cant language judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: The author hoarded up 'gibberish and Billingsgate trash' in his memory; the translator should not value himself solely on hitting the words of cant, though such words have their place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproduce coarse or colorful language only where it serves the author's effect; avoid gratuitous vulgarity or slavish copying that harms tone in the target language.
